nodes.text: Promoting process improvement and optimization through equipment simulations in a 3D space.

Digital Twin Software simulates DENSO robots and equipment within a 3D virtual environment. It integrates the "realvirtual.io" software, which is designed for building digital twin spaces, with "Unity," the world's leading 3D development platform. It can help improve and optimize processes, such as verifying layouts without purchasing any actual equipment, training workers, and reducing setup adjustment time.
Overview of digital twin component software

Unity is the world's most popular platform for 3D development. In addition to its use in game development, Unity now provides the "Unity Industry" application for industrial purposes. As a game creation platform, it is highly effective for building digital twin environments, utilizing advanced 3D technologies and physics.
The world's most popular 3D development platform
A global development platform for creating games and more.
A complete collection of resources to improve digital twin environments.
Utilizes the distinctive 3D capabilities that only a game engine can offer.

Realvirtual.io Professional is a Unity add-on that simplifies the creation of equipment design simulations. With its extensive library of assets, including conveyors and motors, you can intuitively build digital twin environments. It also enables easy simulation of equipment with support for TwinCAT and OPC UA interfaces, PLC connections, and software wiring.

nodes.text: Spark Plug Installation | DENSO Auto Parts

Before attempting to gap any DENSO Iridium Power spark plug, please review the specification chart in the front of this catalog to verify the factory-preset gap. In most cases your Iridium Power plugs do not need to be gapped. Even with small variations in the factory set gap the ultra-efficient firing power design will compensate for those small variations. Should you decide to re-gap your Iridium Power plug, use extreme caution as improper gapping may damage or destroy the Iridium center electrode or porcelain center.
Spark Plug Installation | DENSO Auto Parts
Step 1: Use needle nose pliers or spark plug gapping tool to bend the ground strap up to the desired height. DO NOT LET THE PLIERS OR GAPPING TOOL TOUCH THE IRIDIUM CENTER ELECTRODE OR PORCELAIN.
Step 2: Re-check the gap with a calibrated gapping tool.
Step 1: Use the same method as above, however, bend the ground strap down to the desired height. DO NOT LET THE PLIERS OR GAPPING TOOL TOUCH THE IRIDIUM CENTER ELECTRODE OR PORCELAIN.

Step 2: Re-check the gap with a calibrated gapping tool. WARNING: Failure to follow these directions may permanently damage the spark plug. Note: Never use a round gapping tool to check the gap or to increase or decrease the gap setting.

Whenever possible, it is recommended that the spark plug be installed using a torque wrench. If a torque wrench is not available, tighten in the following manner:

• The threaded area of the cylinder head must be clean.
• Finger-tighten the spark plug into the cylinder head. With a plug wrench, tighten about 1/4 to 1/2 turn (about 1/16 turn for a taper seat plug).
Spark Plug Installation | DENSO Auto Parts
• Over-tightening may cause distortion of the plug housing and in extreme cases, engine damage. Therefore, proper installation is important for the spark plug's performance and life.
The table on this page gives the recommended torque for proper spark plug installation. Improper installation may cause poor performance, and even result in engine damage.

Note: The installation torque values shown above apply to new spark plugs without lubricating the threads. If threads are lubricated, the torque value should be reduced by approximately 1/3 to avoid overtightening.

Iridium Racing® Spark Plug Components | DENSO Auto Parts

Platinum has a higher melting point than the nickel alloys used in conventional spark plug ground electrodes. This feature reduces wear and problems such as melting the ground electrode under severe driving or race conditions. In addition, the platinum alloy used in the 0.8mm ground electrode is produced without the need for fusing or bending, which increases durability and virtually eliminates residual stress.

A small gap has been developed around the tip of the center electrode and insulator. If the plug develops carbon build-up and bridging occurs, electrical discharges in this section burn away any carbon deposits and cleans the insulator. This technology has been patented by DENSO (Japanese patent No. 2727558).
Iridium Racing® Spark Plug Components | DENSO Auto Parts

For racing vehicles, starting problems caused by carbon deposits and bridged plugs before the start of a race can be fatal. To prevent this, a film of silicone oil is applied to the insulator. The water repellent properties of silicone oil keep the insulator surface free from moisture and carbon to prevent any losses in plug insulating performance.
Iridium Racing® Spark Plug Components | DENSO Auto Parts

nodes.text: The bevel on the side of the housing has been increased in size to improve resistance to abnormal combustion. Furthermore, they also make possible the discharge of residual gases and entry of fresh gases; improve self-cleaning performance, which helps reduce fouling of the plug.
360° laser welding* is used to create a seal so reliable the electrode resists wear even in the harshest driving conditions.
* DENSO patented the 360° laser welding method in Japan and the United States. (Japanese patent No. 2921524, U.S. patent pending).
Through DENSO's involvement in motorsports, we have engineered a new insulator that is 20% stronger than insulators previously used.
G. ULTRA-FINE 0.4-MM DIAMETER IRIDIUM CENTER ELECTRODE

The new DENSO Iridium alloy, with an extremely high melting point, is used to create the world's smallest center electrode allowing the voltage requirements to be significantly reduced and greatly improving ignition performance.
This new Iridium alloy achieves its particular characteristics through a unique material structure (*1) and production method (*2).
*1 Small amounts of rhodium are added to the alloy to increase high-temperature oxidation resistance. (Japanese patent 2877035, U.K. patent 23023767)
*2 A fusion method is used to form the center electrode, instead of the conventional sintering method. (Japanese patent 3000955, U.S. patent 5977695)

nodes.text: Poor Cooling Performance in a Vehicle with Dual A/C
Poor Cooling Performance in a Vehicle with Dual A/C | DENSO Auto Parts

CONDITION: Poor cooling performance in a vehicle with a dual (front/rear) A/C system. The system uses a joint type expansion valve* in the rear cooling unit, with no magnetic valve. The compressor has been confirmed to be ok, and the front expansion valve was replaced recently.

CAUSE: The thermosensitive tube of the rear expansion valve has become loose and is not reading the evaporator outlet temperature accurately. This caused the expansion valve to open more than necessary, and caused more refrigerant to flow to the rear cooling unit.

CORRECTION: Access the thermosensitive tube of the rear expansion valve and secure it tightly to the appropriate groove on the low-pressure tube of the rear cooling unit. Consult the manufacturer's service information to meet proper insulation requirements.

nodes.text: Compressor Snap Ring Installation Precaution | DENSO Auto Parts
Compressor Snap Ring Installation Precaution | DENSO Auto Parts
CONDITION: Following A/C compressor installation (with magnetic clutch R&R), compressor is noisy and cooling performance is poor.
CAUSE: It's possible that the snap ring used to secure the stator and rotor was improperly installed.
CORRECTION: Snap rings with a beveled edge must be installed with the beveled edge facing away from the compressor. The snap ring must be fully seated and retain the stator and rotor securely.

A/C Clutch Inoperative and A/C Light Flashing | DENSO Auto Parts
CONDITION: The vehicle A/C is inoperative, compressor clutch will not engage and A/C light is flashing.
CAUSE: The magnetic clutch relay is disengaging, causing the clutch to disengage and the A/C light to flash.
CORRECTION: Toyota has developed a new magnetic clutch relay for this application*.
If the vehicle is exhibiting the symptoms previously described and the relay Toyota P/N is 90987-02022, replace it with a new relay (Toyota P/N 90987-02028).

*May also be seen in various models which have similar system configurations (e.g. 2002-2004 Toyota Camry; 2001-2004 Toyota Echo; 2001-2004 Toyota Celica; 2002-2004 Toyota 4Runner; 2002-2004 Toyota Corolla; 2003-2004 Toyota Highlander, 2003-2004 Toyota Matrix; 2003-2004 Toyota Sienna; 2003-2004 Toyota Solara).

nodes.text: A/C Clutch Inoperative and Fan Won't Turn Off | DENSO Auto Parts
A/C Clutch Inoperative and Fan Won't Turn Off. Check the Water Temperature Switch.
CONDITION: The vehicle's compressor clutch will not engage and/or the condenser fan motor will not turn off. Historically, a failed temperature switch will result in this scenario.

• With the A/C system on, provide a ground signal to the lead wire of the water temperature switch, the compressor clutch should engage.
• Using a multimeter, check the switch for continuity between the housing and the water temperature switch terminal at room temperature. If the switch is open, it has failed and must be replaced.
CAUSE: The A/C water temperature switch may have been damaged, causing the
A/C Clutch Inoperative and Fan Won't Turn Off | DENSO Auto Parts

CORRECTION: When installing A/C water temperature switch, tighten and torque* the switch using only hand tools with a deep socket. Do not over torque the switch assembly during installation. Do not use air tools because the high-speed ratcheting motion can damage the switch. Be careful not to drop or strike the switch during the installation process. Do not use sealing tape.

nodes.text: With a design that's easy for people to interact with and a small body that's easy to carry so that it can be taken anywhere, COBOTTA is a collaborative robot that can automate work immediately.
Do you need that extra hand? Do you want to leave simple tasks to robots, and make more time for creative work?
This flyer introduces options that are engineered to work with COBOTTA to meet needs like those by expanding the range of possible uses for the robot.

● Camera Built-in Set
• AF Camera (N10-W02)
• End-effector EtherNet Cable
• Camera Stay
Two types of hand tools are available*1. You can also fabricate your own hand tool for use with COBOTTA.
This hand tool is ideal for the basic operations of gripping and releasing.
This tool makes it easy to pick up items via suction, without providing an external air compressor.

By attaching a camera designed specifically for use with COBOTTA to the robot's wrist, you can perform work while detecting the position of target objects. Use the factory default calibration to get up and running right away with no troublesome initial setup process.
This AF camera sets the optimal exposure automatically and eliminates the need to focus manually.
This base plate allows COBOTTA to operate in a freestanding orientation without being mounted. The base plate is divided into two parts, upper side and lower side.
This cable allows to connect an external monitor to COBOTTA via a standard, commercially available VGA cable.
This data cable connects COBOTTA to an external device.
*1: Specify at time of order. *2: Requires a HUB with PoE function. This set includes an End-effector EtherNet Cable and a Camera Stay.
*3: Product launch tentatively scheduled for the end of March 2020.

nodes.text: WINCAPS Plus is a software package that provides the optimal application according to the environment used and the customer, and simplifies everything from robot introduction to design and maintenance.

By embedding commands such as flow control statements (conditional branching) in the robot's path, programming can be performed while visually grasping the robot's movement, making it easy for users who are not familiar with programming language to program.

By specifying the start and end points of the robot's motion, the system will automatically generate a path that avoids obstacles and has the shortest cycle time. The robot's path design, which used to rely on the experience of the user, can be generated scientifically so that both skilled and novice users can operate the robot with the same performance.

Assuming that the path taken by the robot during automatic operation is safe, with no obstacles, the system generates a path that allows the robot to safely return to the origin from the operation path that was automatically collected.
*If you are using RC8, a separate dedicated IPC is required.

Robot Viewer is a 3D viewer that can be used with WINCAPS Plus. It provides a comfortable simulation environment for the WINCAPS Plus product line with enhanced 3D CAD data loading, an object operation environment, and object management.

This software is used in the palletizing/depalletizing process. The shape and dimensions of pallets and loads on the software are input, then automatic calculation is performed and the target position is displayed considering the movable range.

nodes.text: Robot Protective Jacket for Food Processing
Simply fit this jacket over a standard-specification robot to easily and inexpensively automate food manufacturing processes that require cleaning.
Scan here for detailed product information

Compatible robots
VS068/VS087
Compatible controllers
RC8A, RC8
*It can't be used for Communication Interface Flange-A, UL specifications, and Cleanroom type.
Easily fitted to implement low-cost automation of food manufacturing processes

To fit the jacket, simply place it over the robot and tie the drawstrings to hold it in place. Then remove from the robot for cleaning as necessary. Alternatively, the jacket can be secured to a pedestal with a dedicated plate*. It can also be cleaned while fitted to the robot by spraying with water or wiping with a moist cloth.
*Dedicated plate should be supplied by customers.
Compatible with chemicals used in food manufacturing processing
The jacket is resistant to a variety of chemicals, ensuring that it will remain clean and sanitary at all times.
Chemicals to which the jacket is resistant

· Sodium hypochlorite aqueous solution (alkaline)
· Sodium hypochlorite pH conditioning liquid (weakly acidic)
· Alcohol
· Hot water (40 to 100 degree C)
Stow wiring by using the dedicated mounting flange
Since cables can be routed from inside the robot protective jacket for food processing through holes in the mounting flange, robot hand cables can be stowed inside the jacket.

nodes.title: Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation
Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation

nodes.text: Shared-Control Teleoperation of Omnidirectional Aerial Robots for Continuous Valve Rotation
Jinjie Li, Yicheng Chen, Haokun Liu, and Moju Zhao

Abstract—Omnidirectional aerial robots offer full 6-DoF independent control over position and orientation, making them popular for aerial manipulation. Although there have been advancements in robotic autonomy, human operation remains essential in complex aerial environments. Previously, we proposed an aerial teleoperation system [1] that brings the rotational flexibility of human hands into the unbounded aerial workspace, which was evaluated through a vertically mounted valve-turning task. However, due to the limited range of human forearm’s motion, the robot could not continuously rotate the valve, hindering its application in industry. In this work, we propose an approach to initiate continuous rotation when the forearm angle exceeds a threshold. This switch of control authority exemplifies the concept shared control from human-robot interaction, marking a further step in aerial teleoperation.

Aerial manipulation is gaining popularity due to its ability to operate freely in 3D space, particularly in high-altitude environments that are difficult for humans to access [2]–[4]. Although fully autonomous manipulation remains the ultimate goal for robotics researchers, the complexity of the aerial environment necessitates keeping a human operator in the loop [5]. In our previous work [1], we proposed a six-degree-of-freedom teleoperation framework for aerial manipulation. Specifically, we designed four interaction modes for different tasks, including Spherical Mode and Cartesian Mode for long-range movement, Operation Mode for precise manipulation, and Locking Mode for temporary pauses, where hand gestures were utilized for seamless mode switching. The proposed framework was evaluated through a valve-turning task1, and to the best of our knowledge, this was the first time the rotational dexterity of the human wrist was intuitively demonstrated on an omnidirectional aerial robot. However, due to the limitations of both the controller and the physical structure of human forearm, we were not able to achieve continuous rotation.

In this work, we introduce the concept of shared control [6] from the human–machine interaction (HMI) domain into aerial operations and design a mechanism to temporarily shift control authority to the robot for continuous valve turning. The approach is briefly introduced as follows, and its performance is evaluated in a real-world experiment.
The teleoperation system for an omnidirectional aerial robot consists of four main elements, as shown in Fig. 1:
All members come from DRAGON Lab, Department of Mechanical Engineering, The University of Tokyo, Tokyo 113-8656, Japan (email: <email>)

Fig. 1. A human operator controls an omnidirectional aerial robot to continuously turn a vertically mounted valve. The robot is in Operation Mode, where its target pose is in general mapped directly from the operator’s hand pose. When the forearm rotation exceeds a threshold, continuous 360° rotation is triggered. The link of video: https://youtu.be/JuPAP6E4yR4.
(1) a human operator, (2) motion-tracking marker sets to localize the hand, (3) a data glove to capture hand gestures, and (4) an omnidirectional aerial robot.

To thoroughly exploit the omnidirectionality of the human hand, an aerial robot capable of hovering in any orientation is required. Here, we use an omnidirectional upgrade of the tiltable quadrotor presented in [7]. The control method is actuator-level NMPC, with an upgrade to handle singularities during continuous rotation.
We define the body frame \{\mathcal{B}\} of the drone at its center of gravity (CoG). With the flight controller, the robot can be simplified as a first-order model:

where \mathbf{p}_B, \mathbf{p}_{Bc}, {}_B^W \mathbf{q}, and {}_B^W \mathbf{q}_c represent current position, target position, current quaternion, and target quaternion, respectively, \circ refers to quaternion multiplication, * refers to conjugation, as well as \mathbf{t}_p and \mathbf{t}_q denote time constants determined by the control performance. The estimated position and orientation are denoted as \hat{\mathbf{p}}_B and {}_B^W \hat{\mathbf{q}}.

We also require the hand’s position \hat{\mathbf{p}}_H and orientation {}_H^W \hat{\mathbf{q}} to determine the robot’s target pose, which is obtained by Motion Capture System. The interaction framework functions as a planning module, aiming to calculate \mathbf{p}_{Bc} and {}_B^W \mathbf{q}_c based on the operator’s action.
We define an Operation Mode in [1], in which we aim to establish an intuitive connection between the drone and the operator’s hand. In summary, we map the pose of the hand
to the robot through the following equations:

The algorithm to trigger the continuous vertical rotation is listed in Alg. 1. In fact, shifting control authority to the robot is not challenging. In contrast, the most challenging part is determining when the control authority should be returned to the operator. Teleoperation systems should be resilient to users' incorrect actions, including tremors and involuntary reflexes. However, when something goes wrong during manipulation, the operator should always know how to move the robot out of danger. In our case, we first use quaternion error to ensure there is no singularity problem in any situation, and then maintain the operator's control over position throughout the process. We also ensure that the robot stops rotating if the orientation of the robot and hand become too close. We found that the robot's behavior after autonomous turning is critical: if the robot suddenly jumps to the pose mapped from the hand, the operator may be startled. Hence, we try to set the stop orientation as close as possible to the hand.

Fig. 2. Data of valve turning. When the rotation of the human hand exceeds a threshold, the robot begins continuous rotation, with the range plotted as a green forward-slash area. The yellow area highlights the period when the robot is attached to the valve. Wrench estimation was shut down for safety. The RMSEs are: p_x: 0.0690 m, p_y: 0.0622 m, p_z: 0.0468 m; roll: 7.8917^\circ, pitch: 9.0527^\circ, yaw: 4.1610^\circ.

We used a fork as the end-effector for valve turning, and an operator used the hand to control the robot. Since continuous valve rotation exceeds the natural flexibility of the human wrist and forearm, we introduced a shared-control approach: when the operator's hand rotation went beyond a threshold, the robot performed continuous vertical rotation for 360^\circ. Although the attitude was governed, the position was always controlled by the operator for safety. As our framework did not include impedance control, the wrench compensation was also shut down to avoid excessive internal forces during turning. The experimental data are shown in Fig. 2.

From Fig. 2, we can see that the robot can continuously rotate the vertically mounted valve. We observed an offset in position when the valve was engaged, indicating possible internal forces. Since the valve is rigid, internal forces accumulated through imperfect alignment may damage the end-effector, highlighting the need for compliance in the future. Additionally, the effector slipped out at the end of the yellow range, possibly due to uneven rotation caused by model error. More accurate calibration of the entire model may help ensure proper engagement.

In this work, we introduced the shared-control concept into our previous system, achieving continuous valve rotation in the real world. In the future, this philosophy could be extended to a general framework for human intent recognition and human-robot collaboration.

[1] J. Li, J. Li, K. Kaneko, H. Liu, L. Shu, and M. Zhao. Six-DoF Hand-Based Teleoperation for Omnidirectional Aerial Robots. [Online]. Available: http://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15009
[2] A. Ollero, M. Tognon, A. Suarez, D. Lee, and A. Franchi, “Past, present, and future of aerial robotic manipulators,” IEEE Trans. Robot., vol. 38, no. 1, pp. 626–645, Feb. 2022.
[3] M. Zhao, K. Nagato, K. Okada, M. Inaba, and M. Nakao, “Forceful valve manipulation with arbitrary direction by articulated aerial robot equipped with thrust vectoring apparatus,” IEEE Robot. Automat. Lett., vol. 7, no. 2, pp. 4893–4900, Apr. 2022.
[4] T. Nishio, M. Zhao, K. Okada, and M. Inaba, “Design, control, and motion planning for a root-perching rotor-distributed manipulator,” IEEE Trans. Robot., vol. 40, pp. 660–676, 2024.
[5] K. Darvish et al., “Teleoperation of humanoid robots: A survey,” IEEE Trans. Robot., vol. 39, no. 3, pp. 1706–1727, Jun. 2023.
[6] M. Selvaggio, M. Cognetti, S. Nikolaidis, S. Ivaldi, and B. Siciliano, “Autonomy in physical human-robot interaction: A brief survey,” IEEE Robot. Automat. Lett., vol. 6, no. 4, pp. 7989–7996, Oct. 2021.
[7] J. Li, J. Sugihara, and M. Zhao, “Servo integrated nonlinear model predictive control for overactuated tiltable-quadrotors,” IEEE Robot. Automat. Lett., vol. 9, no. 10, pp. 8770–8777, Oct. 2024.

▶ High fidelity physics simulator
▶ Realistic sensing
Fuses information from RF & obstacle costs & wireless aware planner over visualization tool

nodes.text: Demo: Closed-Loop Sionna–Isaac Sim Co-Simulation Framework for Wireless-Aware Robot Navigation over ROS 2

Yi Shen Lim, Seungeun Oh, Jihong Park
Singapore University of Technology and Design
Singapore

A robot that offloads its control loop to the network carries the receiver with it, so link quality is decided by where it goes. Simulating this requires both a physics engine and a site-specific propagation model at once; to our knowledge no simulator natively unifies both, with existing couplings of the two limited to offline analyses. We demonstrate a real-time co-simulation framework coupling NVIDIA Isaac Sim and NVIDIA Sionna over ROS 2 that closes the perception–action–communication (PAC) loop between them. Sionna ray-traces the base-station-to-robot channel over the exact geometry Isaac Sim simulates on—rather than modeling it stochastically—and feeds channel states back into the control loop in real time. Ray-traced on GPU, the coverage map is refreshed in \sim 16 ms (\sim 60 Hz), fast enough for real-time control. To showcase the framework’s utility, we implement a wireless-aware navigation application in an OpenStreetMap(OSM)-derived SUTD campus twin with two Nova Carter robots: the closed-loop planner eliminates communication outage at only +7.4\% traversal time over the shortest-path baseline (which spends 7.9 s of its 81.2 s run disconnected).
• Networks → Network simulations; Cyber-physical networks; • Computer systems organization → Robotics; • Computing methodologies → Motion path planning.
Digital twin, ray tracing, closed-loop simulation, co-simulation, wireless-aware motion planning, ROS 2, robotics

Yi Shen Lim, Seungeun Oh, Jihong Park. 2026. Demo: Closed-Loop Sionna–Isaac Sim Co-Simulation Framework for Wireless-Aware Robot Navigation over ROS 2. In The Twenty-seventh International Symposium on Theory, Algorithmic Foundations, and Protocol Design for Mobile Networks and Mobile Computing (MobiHoc '26), November 23–26, 2026, Tokyo, Japan. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 2 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3842721.3850090

Cloud robotics, teleoperation, and autonomous logistics offload perception and decision-making to edge servers, so a robot’s control loop depends on a low-latency wireless link. Link quality varies with the robot’s own position, as structures reflect, diffract, and block the signal. Where the robot goes will decide the connectivity

▶ High fidelity physics simulator
▶ Realistic sensing
Fuses information from RF & obstacle costs & wireless aware planner over visualization tool

Figure 1: Co-simulation view: Isaac Sim simulates robots, Sionna ray-traces channels, ROS 2 relays states, RViz2 (ROS 2’s visualization tool) overlays RSS heatmap and planned routes; attendees drive all views live in Scenario 1.
it gets, coupling planning and communication into one PAC loop [3]. Safe deployment requires a platform where motion and site-specific propagation can be studied, before a robot meets a dead zone.

No single simulator offers this. Robotic simulators lack channel models, and wireless ones (Sionna [4], ns-3) lack physics. Communication-aware planning [5] feeds the planner a statistical channel map; DT-RaDaR [1] ray-traces an OSM/Blender twin with Sionna, as we do, but once and offline, with no physics engine. Robot–network co-simulators [3] close the PAC loop, but over stochastic propagation. Ray-tracing twins such as CAVIAR [2], AODT [6], and SimART [8] are site-specific but close the loop only on communication-side decisions (e.g., beam selection), with mobility given, not planned. None, to our knowledge, combines site-specific ray tracing, a physics engine, and a channel that reaches the motion planner online, at control-loop rates.

We demonstrate a framework that does, coupling NVIDIA Isaac Sim [7] (a GPU-accelerated robotics simulator for physics and sensors) and NVIDIA Sionna [4] (a differentiable wireless ray tracing library) over ROS 2 (Robot Operating System 2, the standard robotics publish–subscribe middleware), inheriting planning (Nav2, ROS 2’s navigation stack), robot interfacing, and visualization (RViz2) from the ROS 2 ecosystem. Isaac Sim, Sionna, and the planner exchange states over ROS 2 as asynchronous nodes. The ray-traced coverage map is published as a standard costmap layer that any ROS 2 planner can consume, and a campus-scale demo quantifies the resulting connectivity–travel-time trade-off.

The difficulty is not running the two simulators in parallel but unifying them: both must share one scene geometry—so the ray-traced map registers cell-for-cell with the navigation grid and a moved obstacle casts physical and RF shadows simultaneously—while loops at milliseconds (ray tracing), tens of milliseconds (physics), and seconds (planning) must interlock without stalling.

© 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).
ACM ISBN 979-8-4007-2975-1/2026/11
https://doi.org/10.1145/3842721.3850090

We resolve the first with a single OSM-derived twin. Its Blender-extruded building footprints serve as Isaac Sim’s physics geometry, Sionna’s ray-tracing scene, and the 0.5 m navigation grid, so ray-traced cells register with navigation cells and moved obstacles updates all three at once. We resolve the second in real-time, running asynchronous, message-triggered ROS 2 nodes (Sec. 2).

(1) Perception: Scene, Physics & State. We rebuild the 540 \times 540 m SUTD campus from OSM footprints via Blender, importing it into Isaac Sim [7], simulating two Nova Carter robots at 3.0 m/s (Fig. 1, left). Poses (physics state) publish over ROS 2 at 60 Hz decoupled from the main loop (Fig. 1, ①). The 0.5 m navigation grid derives from the same twin; onboard sensing adds runtime obstacles.

(2) Communication: Ray Tracing & Coverage. Control flows over the downlink as planning resides on the network. Two 5G base stations (gNodeBs) act as Txs delivering commands to the robot-mounted Rx, each at 18 dBm EIRP in band n78 (3.425 GHz, 50 MHz), mirroring our physical private-5G small cell. Both Txs sit 2.5 m on building facades (marked in Fig. 1); the robot’s vertically polarized dipole Rx (omnidirectional in azimuth) sits at 1.5 m. Sionna RT 2.0.1’s GPU ray tracer [4] runs over the shared geometry (2 \times 10^6 rays, \leq 5 specular reflections) with ITU-R P.2040 concrete, brick, and metal across 48 building meshes and a ground plane. It computes RSS over a coarser 1.5 m grid of candidate Rx positions (360 \times 360 cells). The coverage map is sampled at the robot’s live pose for instantaneous RSS; active Tx–Rx paths are rendered in Sionna’s view (Fig. 1, lower left). Recomputing the map, triggered only by Tx motion or geometry changes, takes \sim 16 ms (9.5–29.5 ms over 5 runs), i.e., \sim 60 Hz (34–105 Hz), and publishes as a ROS 2 OccupancyGrid (Fig. 1, ②). Scope. For scenes, channels are deterministic (RSS varies with position and changes only when the map is re-traced), poses are ground truth, channels are reciprocal, sharing one map, and association is best-server without inter-cell interference.

(3) Action: Wireless-Aware Motion Planning. To demonstrate how the framework closes the PAC loop, we instantiate a wireless-aware navigation application on top of its runtime ROS 2 topics. The threshold RSS_{\min} = -80 dBm is the lowest power at which our link budget (7 dB noise figure, \approx -90 dBm noise floor) sustains the command stream with margin. Each cell takes a wireless cost C_w = \min(254, \frac{254}{\Delta} \max(0, RSS_{\min} - RSS)), with \Delta = 30 dB spanning Nav2’s [0, 254] cost range (free at RSS_{\min}, lethal \Delta below). As a straightforward example to expose the PAC trade-off, we register this layer alongside physical obstacles C_{obs} (static map, detected obstacles, inflation) to give the combined traversal cost:
C_{total}(x, y) = C_{obs}(x, y) + \alpha \cdot C_w(x, y), \quad (1)

which a custom A^* planner searches (accumulating unit step costs per cell), though the framework’s costmap interface can feed arbitrary downstream planners. Here, \alpha = 0 recovers shortest-path planning and larger \alpha buys detours around dead zones. A new search is triggered whenever the costmap changes, and the resulting velocity commands return to Isaac Sim over ROS 2 (Fig. 1, ③), closing the loop that drives Scenario 1’s interactive replanning.
Scenario 1: Interactive Closed-Loop Operation. Attendees set waypoints in the operator view (Fig. 1) over the RSS heatmap;

Figure 2: Routes (a) and RSS along each traversal (b) for \alpha = 0 (red), 10^{-2} (blue), 10^{-1} (green), 1 (black) over the ray-traced coverage map; Tx positions marked, sub-threshold region shaded; outage falls from 7.9 s (red) to 0 s (black).

moving or adding gNodeBs and obstacles into the planned path recomputes the map and exposes handover boundaries. Onboard sensing writes it into C_{obs}, the re-traced map casts its RF shadow into C_w, and the robot detours around both a few seconds later.

System Latency (10 runs). Within the steady-state loop, state ingestion (0.83 ms), Sionna’s ray-tracing kernel (5.53 \pm 0.6 ms once warm; 118 ms initial JIT), and costmap fusion (0.96 ms) deliver updated costmaps in 7.3 ms; the global A^* search dominates, achieving a full loop at 4.73 \pm 0.10 s. Closed-Loop Evaluation. Each robot plans and traverses at 3 m/s in a static scene without halting on link loss, so every \alpha \in \{0, 10^{-2}, 10^{-1}, 1\} yields a complete, comparable traversal (Fig. 2); outage is time below RSS_{\min}. The shortest-path baseline (\alpha = 0) cuts through a building’s RF shadow: 7.9 s of outage over an 81.2 s run. \alpha = 10^{-2} leaves 1.3 s of outage at +1.6% traversal time, and by \alpha = 10^{-1} the route clears the shadow entirely (87.0 s, +7.4%, min. RSS -60.9 dBm); larger \alpha changes little.

Logistics. A single RTX 5090 workstation runs the three views side by side; attendees set goals in the GUI. We bring the workstation and two monitors and need one table (\sim 1.5 \times 0.8 m), three outlets; no network, \sim 30 min setup. Video: https://youtube.com/_TE7tGWxK6A.

nodes.text: Federated Bayesian Surveillance of Mechanical Thrombectomy Adverse Events: A Population Risk Layer for Surgical Digital Twins

Damini Rijhwani
Automation Core Inc., Cambridge, MA, USA
<email> ORCID: 0009-0000-2253-6111

Abstract—Learned surgical simulators and world models can roll out plausible procedural futures, but they carry no grounded estimate of how often interventional devices actually harm patients. We propose treating population-scale adverse-event surveillance as a distinct belief layer of the surgical digital twin, and we evaluate a federated Bayesian protocol for learning it under formal privacy guarantees. Each site holds per-class Gamma-Poisson posteriors over adverse-event rates and exchanges only Rényi-differentially-private natural-parameter updates. We benchmark on the complete FDA MAUDE cohort for thrombus-retrieval catheters (product code NRY): 8,617 reports, of which 6,491 are classified by transparent keyword rules into five thrombectomy complication classes and partitioned across K=8 manufacturer sites. At a matched privacy budget of (\epsilon \approx 2.09, \delta = 10^{-5}), the conjugate protocol attains a held-out Poisson score of -5.78 per test event versus -26.58 for FedAvg with differential privacy. The non-private federated model also outperforms centralized pooling (+3.19 vs +2.93), evidence that manufacturer-specific complication profiles are real and that federation preserves them. Because MAUDE lacks procedure denominators, outputs are relative rate orderings rather than absolute risks, and we report all privacy-utility operating points.
Index Terms—surgical digital twin, adverse-event surveillance, federated learning, differential privacy, mechanical thrombectomy, Bayesian inference

Surgical robotics is increasingly adopting world models, using learned simulators to predict action outcomes before execution. World foundation models now evaluate surgical robot policies in silico [1], digital twins are proposed to ground foundation models in operating rooms [2], [3], and surgical digital twin research is developing rapidly [4]. Endovascular intervention, especially mechanical thrombectomy, is a primary target of this effort.

These systems share a clear blind spot. A learned simulator can predict that a retriever will deform a vessel, but cannot estimate how often retrievers of that class perforate vessels in clinical practice, since that information resides in fragmented, sensitive post-market records rather than surgical video. Real-world failure statistics for thrombectomy devices exist in scattered form: registry studies of the FDA Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database document device-specific complication patterns in peripheral and pulmonary procedures [5], [6], with reproducibility remaining an active concern [7]. Individual hospitals rarely see enough
events to estimate rates reliably, and procedural records cannot be centralized.

We propose that surgical digital twins require a distinct population risk layer: calibrated beliefs over adverse-event rates by device class and complication type, learned across institutions without transferring raw records, to condition per-procedure simulations. This paper introduces this layer and evaluates it on real public data:

1) A federated Bayesian surveillance protocol. Sites maintain per-class Gamma-Poisson posteriors and exchange only Rényi-differentially-private (RDP) natural-parameter updates of dimension 2Z per round. Conjugacy reduces each update to a two-scalar sufficient statistic per class instead of a gradient.
2) A thrombectomy benchmark from complete public data. We provide the recipe for a manufacturer-federated partition of the complete MAUDE cohort for thrombus-retrieval catheters: 8,617 reports, with 6,491 classified into five complication classes across major thrombectomy manufacturers.
3) Evidence that federation preserves manufacturer heterogeneity. The federated per-site model outperforms centralized pooling even in the absence of privacy noise, indicating that complication profiles differ across device makers, a structure that pooled models erase.

Scope. This paper evaluates population-level rate estimation on public surveillance data. It does not evaluate per-procedure simulation, device control, or clinical decision-making, and its outputs are not evidence of comparative device safety.
For complication class z \in \{1, \dots, Z\} at site k, the event count over exposure n_{z,k} is modeled as conditionally Poisson with latent rate \theta_z:

The posterior update is conjugate: with natural parameter \eta_z = (\alpha_z - 1, -\beta_z)^\top, a site's contribution is the sufficient statistic \Delta\eta_{z,k} = (y_{z,k}, -n_{z,k})^\top, and the global posterior is the prior plus the sum of site contributions:
This estimator family extends the Bayesian shrinkage framework of pharmacovigilance signal detection [8], [9] to a multi-site setting where no party inspects the pooled table.

Each round, every site clips its update to norm C, adds Gaussian noise \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I/K), and transmits under pairwise-masking secure aggregation [10], ensuring the server observes only the noised sum. Sensitivity is bounded by the event-level neighboring relation: one report perturbs one class count while exposure windows remain fixed, so \|\Delta\eta\|_2 \leq 1 \leq C. Privacy is tracked in RDP [11] with additive composition over T rounds and conversion to (\varepsilon, \delta) [12]; sufficient-statistic perturbation for conjugate models follows [13]. Per-round communication requires 2Z scalars per site, independent of cohort size, unlike gradient-based federated methods [14], [15], [16].

In our experiments, each round releases the statistic of an independent Bernoulli-subsampled batch (fraction 1/20) over T=200 rounds. Counts and exposures accumulate together, so posterior means remain unbiased, and the evaluation below depends only on posterior means. Accumulated precision would overstate effective sample size by T/20 and must be renormalized before interpreting posterior widths. The accountant charges every release and claims no subsampling amplification.

We retrieved the complete openFDA MAUDE cohort for product code NRY (catheter, thrombus retriever): 8,617 reports through August 2026, queried by authoritative product code with full pagination and archived query manifests. Report narratives are categorized by transparent, severity-ordered keyword rules into Z=5 classes: vessel perforation or dissection (1,293), hemorrhage (1,706), distal embolization (307), device fracture or detachment (2,806), and failure to retrieve or track (379), with 6,491 reports matching at least one class. Sites represent the top K-1=7 manufacturers by classified report volume, capturing the major thrombectomy vendors (Penumbra, Micro Therapeutics/ev3, Neuravi, Concentric Medical, Covidien, Stryker Neurovascular), plus an OTHER site (K=8). Exposure n_{z,k} is the site reporting-year span, and 20% of events per site are held out.

Estimand. MAUDE is voluntary surveillance lacking procedure denominators. Fitted rates represent events per reporting-year; outputs are relative rate orderings across classes and sites rather than absolute complication probabilities, and reporting propensities vary across manufacturers.

We compare against centralized pooled Gamma estimation, FedAvg, FedAvg with DP-SGD-style noise, FedProx, SCAFFOLD, and FedPA, all optimizing the same intercept-only Poisson objective, with T=200, C=\sqrt{2}, \delta=10^{-5}, and

TABLE I
HELD-OUT POISSON SCORE PER TEST EVENT ON THE MAUDE THROMBECTOMY FEDERATION (K=8, Z=5, 10 SEEDS, 95% BOOTSTRAP CI). HIGHER IS BETTER; ONLY DIFFERENCES ARE INTERPRETABLE.

Method	Privacy	Score
Centralized (pooled Gamma)	none	+2.93 [+2.91, +2.94]
FedAvg	none	—26.58 [—26.58, —26.58]
FedProx	none	−26.58 [−26.58, −26.58]
SCAFFOLD	none	−26.58 [−26.58, −26.58]

Federated conjugate, \sigma=96	\epsilon \approx 1.02	−8.43 [−10.26, −6.68]

Fig. 1. Per-class Gamma posterior rate intervals (95%) for the four largest manufacturer sites, non-private fit, flat prior. Rates are events per reporting-year from voluntary reports: relative orderings under differing reporting propensities, not evidence of comparative device safety. Profiles differ markedly across manufacturers, which is the heterogeneity that pooling erases.

\sigma \in \{6, 12, 24, 48, 96\}. The metric is the unnormalized held-out Poisson log-likelihood per test event (higher is better); only differences across methods are interpretable. Results are reported as means over 10 seeds with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

Conjugate updates outperform gradient federation at matched privacy. At (\varepsilon \approx 2.09, \delta=10^{-5}), the conjugate protocol scores -5.78 versus -26.58 for FedAvg+DP (Table I). Gradient baselines fail to move from their initialization on this objective; all five gradient rows, private and non-private alike, remain at -26.58 with degenerate confidence intervals. Because no learning-rate search was performed, these rows represent an unoptimized floor rather than tuned competitors. The supported claim is that closed-form sufficient-statistic exchange outperforms gradient optimization for this model class on these data, not that it surpasses well-tuned federated systems.

Manufacturer heterogeneity is genuine, and federation preserves it. The non-private federated model outperforms centralized pooling (+3.19 vs +2.93), and Fig. 1 illustrates why. Pooling assumes a single complication profile for all devices; the data contradict this, aligning with the clinical distinction between aspiration and stent-retriever mechanisms and with device-specific MAUDE findings [5], [6]. This inverts the typical framing: federation here is not a privacy-constrained compromise of a centralized ideal, but the better-specified model.

Privacy-utility frontier. Utility decreases monotonically with added noise, from +0.47 at \epsilon \approx 21.55 to -8.43 at \epsilon \approx 1.02. We report all operating points so deployments can select target budgets explicitly.

Limitations. MAUDE is voluntary and under-reports true incidence; reporting propensities vary by manufacturer and over time, and MAUDE query reproducibility is a recognized challenge [7]. Keyword classification is transparent but coarse: 25% of reports match no class, and narrative quality varies. The privacy guarantee operates at the event level, assuming an honest-but-curious server without collusion. The evaluation scores per-site posteriors; practical deployment would require formal data-use agreements and prospective calibration assessments at the chosen operating budget.

The population layer examined here supplies priors rather than procedural dynamics. A natural extension is coupling this layer with a per-procedure belief-state twin: posterior rate beliefs conditioned on device class initialize the risk state of an intra-operative world model, which updates from sparse observations (such as pulsed fluoroscopy) and evaluates posterior-predictive risk for candidate actions before execution. That direction, aligned with twin-grounded foundation-model control [2], [1], remains future work; this paper provides the underlying population layer learned across institutions under formal privacy guarantees.
Code and data. The benchmark recipe, classification rules, and protocol implementation will be released upon publication; all data are public (openFDA MAUDE) [17].

nodes.title: Bootstrap method to speed up grasp generation [6]:

nodes.text: Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments
Mathilde Kappel, Mahdi Khoramshahi, Louis Annabi, Faiz Ben Amar, Stéphane Doncieux
Sorbonne Université, CNRS, Institut des Systèmes Intelligents et de Robotique (ISIR), Paris, France

Abstract—We propose to use Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms to solve robotic prehensile manipulation tasks in open-ended environments. Our approach enables the efficient discovery of a wide range robust grasp configurations, which serve as reliable starting points for generating diverse prehensile manipulation trajectories on articulated objects. The resulting diversity in manipulation behaviors enhances generalization and adaptability, enabling effective deployment continuously evolving open-world settings.

QDG-Manipulation :
Diversity of prehensile manipulation trajectories
Fig. 1. From Quality-Diversity grasp generation to prehensile manipulation: the QDG-Manipulation pipeline.

Developing algorithms enabling robot prehensile manipulation tasks in dynamic real-world environments remains a major challenge in robotics. The manipulation problem aims at finding a set of suitable robot controls to change the state of an object from an initial to a desired configuration. More specifically, prehensile manipulation involves keeping the object grasped while the whole robot executes the manipulation using its control system [1]. For example opening a fridge is prehensile manipulating switching the object state from closed to open by grasping the fridge hammer during the whole robot motion. Solving robotic prehensile manipulation problems is inherently difficult due to the sparse nature of the grasping problem. In such scenarios, the space of solutions is extremely large, yet successful feedback is rare, making learning-based approaches particularly challenging. Moreover, the environments in which robots operate are highly variable—each static scene can differ significantly in object positions, shapes, levels of clutter, and semantic context [2]. For these reasons, prehensile manipulation is often described as an open-world or open-ended problem.

One promising approach to tackle the complexity of open-world environment problems is using real-time adaptation to the environment based on spontaneous exploration. Curiosity-driven learning and intrinsic motivation methods exist to solve

sparse reward tasks. More specifically, Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms have been designed to efficiently explore large and sparse environments by generating a diverse set of high-quality solutions, rather than converging on a single optimal policy. Precisely, Quality-Diversity algorithms are evolutionary algorithms. Evolutionary algorithms iteratively apply variation, evaluation and selection processes to a population of candidate solutions. QD methods are evolutionary algorithms that additionally optimize the diversity of solutions in the population according to behavior descriptors designed by the user [3].

The objective of our research is to use the Quality-Diversity open-ended learning method [4] to solve a real-world application: prehensile grasp manipulation. First, we generate a diverse repertoire of prehensile grasps, then we use these grasps to generate articulated object manipulation trajectories.

QDG-6DoF grasp module [5]: The QDG-6DoF module takes as input a target object and an end-effector model, and produces as output an archive of 6-DoF grasp poses distributed around the object. This module is built upon the Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithm, in which the core components—namely the genome, population, behavior, and fitness—are specifically adapted to address the challenge of grasping in robotics. In this context, each grasp candidate is

treated as an individual within the population. The genome of an individual encodes the Cartesian position of the end-effector (x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3, its orientation represented as a unit quaternion (q_1, q_2, q_3, q_4), and a synergy component from a predefined synergy space. These parameters define a continuous 6-DoF grasp configuration for the end-effector. The behavior space is designed to reflect the structure of the 3D environment surrounding the articulated object. Each grasp candidate is associated with a behavior descriptor, defined as the voxel in a discretized 3D grid that best approximates the spatial location of the grasp. A deterministic behavior mapping function assigns each individual to a unique cell in this space, effectively partitioning the continuous grasp space into manageable, behaviorally distinct regions. The fitness of an individual corresponds to a success score that evaluates the quality of the grasp, based on whether the proposed configuration achieves a stable and feasible grasp under physical simulation. The objective of the QD module is to construct a MAP-Elites structured archive, in which each cell in the discretized behavior space is populated with the highest-performing grasp candidate among all those projected to that cell. This process relies on local competition, where individuals only compete with others sharing the same behavior descriptor. Such a mechanism promotes both grasp diversity across space and optimality within each spatial region. To efficiently explore the grasp behavior space, the module applies a mutation-selection process that iteratively refines the active population. Individuals are sampled from the archive and mutated to generate new grasp candidates, which are then evaluated and reinserted based on their fitness and behavior descriptor. The search is further guided by physical priors, allowing the projection from the search space to the grasp space to be grounded in physically plausible configurations.
Bootstrap method to speed up grasp generation [6]:

In order to scale up the generation of synthetic grasps using QDG-6DoF, we combine object mesh augmentation with transfer learning from previously acquired grasp repertoires. Starting with a dataset of grasp poses defined over a set of core objects P = (\mathcal{P}_i)_{1 \leq i \leq n}, where n denotes the number of original objects, we apply a mesh augmentation process to each object. This yields an extended dataset P' = (\mathcal{P}_i^a)_{1 \leq i \leq n, 1 \leq a \leq a_{\max}}, where a_{\max} is the number of data augmentations per object. The resulting augmented objects are then provided with a QDG-6DoF process, which is initialized with the grasps found on the reference object.

From grasp to articulated object manipulation: When applied to articulated objects, the QD-Grasp-6DoF module generates a repertoire of diverse and successful grasps across different object parts. These grasps are not only stable but also enable physical interaction. After establishing contact, the robot enters a compliant mode and passively follows the motion induced by the object’s articulation. During execution, the robot switches to active control to replay the trajectory and manipulate the object accordingly. Thus, each grasp is associated with both a stable contact and a dynamic manipulation

Using Quality-Diversity (QD) methods with priors significantly accelerates 6-DoF grasp sampling for prehensile manipulation and enables the construction of large datasets containing diverse and robust grasps. The QDG-6DoF module is compatible with various robotic platforms, ranging from simple parallel 2-finger grippers to highly dexterous hands. Furthermore, the QDG-6DoF framework was extended with a bootstrap method applied to augmented data. As a result, we introduce QDGset, a prehensile grasp dataset comprising 62 million grasps across 5,000 distinct objects—3.5 times larger than the widely used ACRONYM dataset [7].

Beyond grasping, QDGset serves as a rich source of initial configurations for generating diverse manipulation trajectories. The diversity of these trajectories is a direct consequence of the underlying grasp variability provided by QDGset.

This study demonstrates that Quality-Diversity algorithms, originally developed for exploration in sparse and high-dimensional environments, can be effectively applied to solve prehensile manipulation tasks in open-world robotics. By leveraging QD’s capacity to generate a repertoire of diverse and high-quality grasps, we overcome the sparse reward challenge inherent to grasping problems. The diversity is essential in open-domain tasks where a robot must manipulate objects under changing conditions.

We are currently working on incorporating compliant control mechanisms into the way the prehensile manipulation grasps are executed by the robot. The robot should respond intelligently to physical interactions while following the trajectories provided by the Quality-Diversity trajectory repertoire. Such mechanisms not only enhance adaptability and robustness in the face of real-world uncertainties but also have the potential to reduce the sim-to-real gap.

QLAUN: A Research-Oriented, Robust, Agile, Modular, and Affordable Torque-Controlled Quadruped Robot
QLAUN: A Research-Oriented, Robust, Agile, Modular, and Affordable Torque-Controlled Quadruped Robot

nodes.text: QLAUN: A Research-Oriented, Robust, Agile, Modular, and Affordable Torque-Controlled Quadruped Robot
Mohamad S. Moudallal1 and Noel J. Maalouf2

Abstract—QLAUN Bot (Quad-Legged Adaptive Unmanned Navigator Robot) is a torque-controlled quadruped robot that is research-oriented, cost-effective, and aimed at achieving simultaneous robustness and agility while being completely 3D-printed. It is a quadruped robot that is aimed at empowering robotics research at universities and research institutes in Lebanon and the MENA region. Using a novel electronics-free leg design strategy, we present a modular robot with interchangeable and easily replaceable legs. The 15 kg robot possesses 12 DoF (Degrees-of-Freedom) with three per leg, each paired with a completely 3D-printed Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD) actuator that consists of a brushless DC motor and a low-ratio gearbox transmission that is connected to a belt transmission system for significantly increasing the torque outputs at the joints. We present legs that have decoupled hip and knee actuators to improve the overall modularity of the robot. QLAUN is almost completely 3D-printed using polylactic acid (PLA) and assembled using off-the-shelf parts to create a robust, agile, and affordable robot for legged robot locomotion research. The legs possess joints with wide ranges of motion, including a continuous hip flexion-extension joint. A compliant foot, printed using TPU-95A is also implemented for alleviating hard impacts and handling terrain uncertainties. This extended abstract aims to introduce QLAUN, a novel platform for robotics research, emphasizing the design concepts and principles that underpin its development to the academic and research communities in the field of robotics.

Quadruped robots have existed for some time, with one of the earliest actively actuated models dating back to 1986 with Marc Raibert’s quadruped robot [4]. Raibert made significant contributions to the field through his work on leg design, single-leg modeling, and leg control. Over time, quadruped robots have become lighter, faster, and more durable, with improved perception of their surroundings. The development of quadruped robots is a multi-disciplinary process that requires significant resources and effort in areas such as mechanical engineering, locomotion control, perception, and path planning. However, the most critical aspect of the development process is the mechanical design, as it dictates the passive locomotion model of the robot.
Research on quadruped robotics has extensively explored various leg configurations, each offering distinct advantages
Fig. 1: Visual Comparison between Marc Raibert’s Quadruped Robot [4] and QLAUN

for locomotion dynamics and stability. Mainly, three types dominate the field. Prismatic legs are foundational, characterized by their two degrees of freedom (DoF); a revolute joint at the hip and a linear joint connecting the shank to the thigh. This configuration, prominently featured in the pioneering legged robots developed by Marc Raibert [4], set a precedent for early robotic designs. Articulated legs, that incorporate two DoF at both the hip and knee, represent an evolution in design, providing greater flexibility and control. Extending this concept further, redundant articulated legs introduce an additional joint and link, akin to the anatomical structure of an ankle and foot in quadruped animals [5].
Research on legged robotic systems is generally financially challenging for smaller institutions with small to almost no funding. Open-source quadruped robots that are designed
Presented as an Extended Abstract at the IEEE ICRA@40 Anniversary Conference, Rotterdam, Netherlands, September 2024.
This work was supported by the PIRF-I0022 grant through the President’s Intramural Research Fund at the Lebanese American University.
1Mohamad S. Moudallal is the corresponding author and is with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Lebanese American University, Byblos, Lebanon. <email>
2Noel J. Maalouf is with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Lebanese American University, Byblos, Lebanon. <email>

for robotics research have been proven to be useful when it comes to investigating and advancing locomotion principles, especially with robots like the robot SOLO from the Open Dynamic Robot Initiative [1]. SOLO is an open-source quadruped robot that is research-oriented, affordable, and very lightweight with a total weight of 2.2 kg, making it very agile.

Most quadruped robots focus mainly on agility, speed, and mobility whereas a low payload-to-weight ratio characterizes them. Kirin, a quasi-direct-drive actuated quadruped robot with prismatic legs, weighs 50 kg and can handle loads up to 125 kg [6]. In an analysis done by Y. Zhou et al., the payload-to-weight ratios of the well-known quadruped robots in the industry are presented. All showcased systems feature a payload capacity that is less than 100%, except for Kirin. Nevertheless, Kirin is a payload-focused robot with prismatic legs augmenting the payload-carrying capacity of the robot, while decreasing the agility of the system dramatically. Kirin has agility and mobility that is nowhere near the ones achieved by agility-oriented quadruped robots such as StarLETH, ANYmal, and Boston Dynamics’ Spot, among others [6].

Systems that accomplish versatility and efficiency at the same time as well as payload-to-weight ratios higher than unity are scarce. There is minimal research on the differences between leg topologies. There is little to no research on leg design alterations between the fore and hind legs with most of them being limited to minor length, angle, or orientation changes [2]. Moreover, the field fails to provide a low-cost 3D-printed mechanical robotic quadruped leg that is both robust and agile.

Henceforth, we present QLAUN (Quad-Legged Adaptive Unmanned Navigator), a novel 3D-printed, torque-controlled quadruped robot that is research-oriented, affordable, and modular, aiming to achieve a balance between robustness and agility.

The main actuator for QLAUN consists of a brushless DC motor (mjbots MJ5208, 330KV, 600W), a 3D-printed 8:1 planetary gearbox to achieve a Quasi-Direct Drive (QDD), and a high-resolution incremental encoder (AMT 103-V, 2048PPR). The actuator is around 85cm in diameter and 65cm tall. The actuator’s gearbox possesses helical gears, improving torque output and reducing backlash. QLAUN’s actuator is handled and controlled by BLDC drivers that are capable of Field-Oriented Control (ODriveRobotics ODrive Pro). The actuators are operated at 20V and can consume up to 30A from a Li-ion battery. This actuator provides torques of up to 5N.m while limited to 40% of its full power capacity.

We present QLAUN’s leg, called RAPID (Robust & Affordable Prototyping of an Inertial Driven) Leg, as a novel, completely 3D-printed, and electronics-free design. It is a 3-DOF leg featuring hip abduction-adduction (HAA), hip

flexion-extension (HFE), and knee flexion-extension (KFE) joints. The thigh and shank are dimensioned with a 1:1 ratio, as observed in canine mammals [3]. RAPID features decoupled hip (HFE) and knee (KFE) joints by using transmission belts. They both have 4:1 ratios bringing the total ratio for these joints to 32:1, thus augmenting the torque. The electronics-free design follows the modularity principle by allowing researchers to swap out the leg for any custom-made leg using three bolts. The leg is printed using polylactic acid (PLA), assembled with off-the-shelf parts, and features a compliant foot, printed with TPU-95A.

QLAUN’s design philosophy embraces modularity not only in its functional aspects but also in its structural components. The robot’s 3D-printed chassis enables a high degree of customization, accommodating everything from specialized sensor arrays to complex manipulator arms. This adaptability makes QLAUN an ideal platform for a broad spectrum of robotics experiments, catering to specific research needs across various domains. Weighing approximately 15 kg and measuring 38 cm tall, 77 cm long, and 38 cm wide, QLAUN combines a compact and manageable size with a durable structure that is conducive to both laboratory and real-world applications. Its versatile design simplifies the process of exploring different leg topologies and sensor integrations, thereby accelerating innovation in robotic mobility and interaction with environments.

Designed to enhance legged locomotion studies, QLAUN offers a robust, agile, and affordable platform that promotes diverse experimental studies, beginning at the Lebanese American University and extending across the MENA region. QLAUN is set to support advanced research projects, including robust locomotion, SLAM technologies, and terrain analysis. Furthermore, QLAUN will also be available as a ready-made product and as an open-source initiative, providing its designs and software to the global research community to foster innovation and practical applications.

Right: two cameras split the roles: a front-facing fisheye camera gives the wearer wide-angle eyes, keeping a reaching hand in view until it lands, while a rear RGB camera (with a thermal companion) senses that touch as a shadow on the back-lit skin.

Floating things invite touch. We present Feelium, a blimp-based telepresence platform that enables visual embodiment and touch interaction through its inflatable skin. Through a VR headset, a remote person inhabits the blimp, looking out of it first-person, appearing on its skin as a face or avatar, and steering it through
UIST Adjunct '26, November 02–05, 2026, Detroit, MI, USA

the room. Partners in the room pat it, press a palm against it, draw on it, or lean into it; the skin senses each contact, renders it into the wearer’s view in VR spaces. Touch thus provides a physical interaction channel for remote presence, turning the skin into a shared surface between remote and co-located partners.
• Human-centered computing → Interaction devices; Virtual reality.
blimp, telepresence, touch, social touch, virtual reality

George Xi Wang, Henghao Li, Shan Lin, Yunge Wen, Jiaqian Hu, and Yuhua Jin. 2026. Feelium: A Touchable Blimp Body for Aerial Telepresence. In The 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST Adjunct '26), November 02–05, 2026, Detroit, MI, USA. ACM, New York, NY, USA, 3 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3830397.3841870

People reach out to touch what floats beside them: when Abtahi et al. wrapped a quadcopter in a safe-to-touch cage, touch leapt from 1.4% to 38.9% of interactions [3]. However, the system cannot pass the touch back to the person operating the drone. Later haptic and touchable drones kept the same limits: contact stays fingertip-scale and transient, sensing lives in external tracking systems, and the rotors stay loud and dangerous [1, 2, 5, 6, 10].

Blimps are the opposite. They can hover among people for hours and be touched without risk. Two decades of research have explored blimps as carriers and screens: tele-embodiment (PRoP [11]), projected faces [17], flying signage [16], light-field heads (Light-Bee [20]), ultrasound-positioned midair balloons [4], and flapping-wing companions built for closeness rather than input [18, 19]. Across these systems the envelope is output-only. Touchable inflatables do exist on the ground — hemispherical multi-touch displays [14], Embolloon’s unlocalized social touch [8], robot-reeled tangible balloons [12] — yet none connects the touched surface to a remote person. Touch, though, is precisely the channel that deepens mediated closeness, from remote handshakes [9] to cortisol-lowering huggable media and multi-task VR space [13, 15].

Feelium fills this gap: to our knowledge, it is the first to explore envelope touch in an aerial telepresence context. We contribute: (1) the Feelium system, which integrates a flying-display blimp platform, first-person VR inhabitation, and an onboard touch-sensing envelope; (2) a vocabulary of two-party touch interactions between a co-located partner and the remote person inside; and (3) a preliminary technical validation of touch sensing on an inflatable envelope.

Blimp. Feelium’s body is a 64 cm indoor helium blimp. Most of the envelope is blackened to retain helium and reject ambient light; the light-scattering front face is a rear-projection screen, lit from inside by a 24.9 g laser projector (Ultimems HD309) through a 180° fisheye lens. Four motors under closed-loop control hold a quiet, stable hover among people, and the complete body weighs 323.7 g against ~360 g of buoyant lift.

VR. A remote person puts on an Apple Vision Pro and becomes the blimp (Figure 1, left). A front-facing fisheye camera serves as the wearer’s eyes; its wide field keeps a partner’s reaching hand in view all the way to contact, so a touch arrives on screen rather than out of frame. The wearer’s face or animated avatar is displayed on the envelope so partners see who is inside. Six motion commands (forward, backward, up, down, turn left, turn right) let the wearer drift, turn, and station the body in the room; control, video, and speech all travel over HTTP.

Touch. A press from outside casts a shadow in the projector’s back-light. A second camera at the rear of the blimp (a Raspberry Pi AI Camera, Sony IMX500) watches the membrane from inside, paired with a 32×24 MLX90640-D55 thermal camera (Figure 1, right). The two split the roles cleanly: the RGB camera makes every touch decision, while the thermal camera senses only presence. The RGB shadow pipeline [7] keeps a slowly adapting reference image of the untouched, back-lit membrane and computes per-pixel relative shadow depth: the fraction of back-light lost against that reference, which makes the signal independent of the projector’s uneven brightness. A shadow counts as touch when it passes either of two gates. An instant depth gate catches firm presses. A sustained-anchoring gate takes the rolling minimum of shadow depth over the past second: a pressing fingertip stays pinned to the membrane, while a hovering hand wobbles and its shadow momentarily thins. The fingertip is localized as the centroid of the shadow’s darkening core. A tracker then segments the per-frame decisions into discrete events (onset to release, with debouncing), distinguishing tap, hold, and swipe by contact duration and fingertip path length. The thermal camera complements this. Each frame is differenced against a slowly adapting ambient baseline, and a cluster of pixels a few degrees above it reads as a warm body, letting the blimp notice a hand or partner drawing near before and between contacts. Thermal frames carry no touch decision (conducted heat through the membrane is too weak and slow). Each detected touch is rendered as a located marker in the wearer’s first-person view, and the projector answers at the touched spot.

The skin’s contact primitives, composed over time and area, turn everyday gestures into conversation between the partner in the room and the person inside. Greeting pat: taps on the “head” ripple into the wearer’s view; the envelope returns a warm pulse. Palm-to-palm: the wearer raises a hand to meet a palm-shaped glow, two prints merging — held hands without hands. Peck tap: a tap at the “cheek” blooms a small heart; the wearer can pinch to send one back. Finger-drawing guess: strokes render live in the wearer’s view, and a correct guess ignites the drawing. Lean-in hug: sustained large-area contact sets the whole skin glowing in a slow breathing rhythm. Wearer-initiated: a projected shimmer invites the partner’s hand, and small motion replies (a drift closer, a gentle bounce) let the body respond. These exchanges suit settings where presence, not information, is the payload: a goodnight palm-press in a couple’s daily call, a drawing game with a child before bed, or a distant relative drifting through a family gathering as a body people can pat hello.
Feelium: A Touchable Blimp Body for Aerial Telepresence
UIST Adjunct '26, November 02–05, 2026, Detroit, MI, USA
Figure 2: Sustained-anchoring score on labelled contact and hover clips: contact stays almost entirely above the fitted threshold; hover keeps dipping below.

We validated the skin on recordings from the real blimp (Figure 2): 228 labelled trials over three sessions – 138 prompted touches (78 taps, 24 holds, 36 swipes) and 90 negatives (30 hovers, 30 no-contact hand disturbances, 30 empty scenes) – plus three continuous ~75 s clips (steady contact, hovering, empty). Detection: the shadow detector is sensitive: with a hand present (touching or not), it registered activity in 171 of 198 trials, and it never fired in the 30 empty scenes. The hard decision is therefore not seeing the hand but rejecting near-hovers: thresholding the darkened area alone reaches 95% recall but only 77% precision, because a hand hovering just above the membrane darkens it almost as much as a touch. The sustained-anchoring gate closes this gap: on the continuous clips its score separates contact from hover at AUC 0.99, and a threshold fit on the first 60% of each clip holds 0.90 balanced accuracy on the unseen remainder. Localization: the 69 taps and holds with a detected landing point cluster tightly by prompted target (RMS spread 4–21 px, median 9 px in the detector’s 640 \times 480 working resolution); coordinates are camera-space, as screen-to-camera calibration is future work. The pipeline runs onboard at ~15 fps. Current limits: results are from dim-room lighting and one rectangular “sensitive skin patch” of the envelope.

Feelium enables touchable, inhabitable aerial telepresence, integrating an onboard touch-sensing envelope with first-person VR embodiment for two-party social touch. A preliminary technical validation provided early evidence of the system’s feasibility and potential, motivating a dyadic evaluation of social presence with the full touch loop as well as whole-envelope sensing, haptic feedback to the wearer, and gesture-piloted flight. Running fully onboard a quiet indoor blimp, this work hopes to give remote presence a body that invites touch, bringing separated partners and families within arm’s reach.

nodes.text: Risk-Aware Kinodynamic Motion Planning Under Uncertainty For Safe Navigation on Planetary Environments
Sachin Sunil Kelkar1, Tanmay Dokania1, Yashwanth Kumar Nakka1

Abstract—For autonomous space exploration, robotic agents need to perform motion planning in which environmental interactions may be unknown. Learning these interactions, such as terrain mechanics for wheeled robots, can introduce uncertainties that lead to risky motion plans and potentially hazardous operations or mission failures. Moreover, uncertainties induced by perception-based systems can exacerbate the problem of safe motion planning. In this letter, we address the problem of performing cost-optimal kinodynamic motion planning with risk awareness. We approach this in two steps. First, a sampling-based planner (AO-RRT) generates a dynamically feasible and risk-aware asymptotically cost-optimal trajectory. Second, we formulate motion planning as a nonlinear optimization problem and solve it using sequential convex programming (SCP), using the AO-RRT trajectory as an initial solution. By quantifying risk using conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), we demonstrate a reduction in risk by over ~97% across trajectories in simulation and hardware experiments.

Risk-aware motion planning is the problem of constructing a feasible trajectory for a robot to follow around obstacles while accounting for uncertainties arising from various sources. It is critically important for autonomous space exploration, where robotic agents traverse uncertain environments, with actuation degradation and unmodeled terrain dynamics. A planner that does not account for these uncertainties can lead to mission-critical failure or hazardous operations [1]. In previous works, uncertainty in the environment and sensor model are considered to generate risk-aware geometric trajectories [2] or modeled as a function of terrain features [3]. A two-step approach in [4] tracks a risk-neutral geometric plan with a CVaR-constrained controller. We consider quantifying the uncertainty in the learned dynamics model used by the planner to generate a risk-aware initial trajectory.

To address these problems, our contributions are: (1) Quantify uncertainty in the learning-based dynamics model using conformal prediction, (2) Formulate AO-RRT with closed-loop risk computation as cost, (3) Cast the nonlinear problem as locally convex and optimize for CVaR and control cost in the given AO-RRT homotopy, guaranteeing the nonlinear dynamics are followed.
We consider the following uncertain dynamics model, [5].
1Authors are with the Daniel Guggenheim School of Aerospace Engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, 30332 USA. Email: [skelkar37, tdokania3, ynakka3]@gatech.edu

Fig. 1: For the same initial conditions and obstacle uncertainty space, AO-RRT with risk cost generates an initial trajectory solution for Sequential Convex Programming that has less joint collision risk

here x \in \mathbb{R}^n, u \in \mathbb{R}^m, d(x, u) \in \mathbb{R}^n are the system state, control input, and the unmodeled dynamics residue term. We model the system as a first-order velocity-controlled model with states, v = [v_x, \omega]^T, and control u = [v_{\text{cmd}}, \omega_{\text{cmd}}]^T. We learn and approximate the residual term using a Lipschitz-continuous neural network as d(v, u) \approx \Phi(v)u.

To quantify the uncertainty of the neural network’s output and incorporate it into motion planning, we use conformal prediction [6] by computing the error between the predicted residual dynamics and the ground truth measured with a motion capture system. Hence, we obtain the set \mathcal{M},
here l, e_{\min/\max} are the minimum and maximum error in the linear and angular acceleration residual terms, computed at the 95% confidence level.

We quantify proximity to the boundaries of uncertain obstacles as a risk field over \mathbb{R}^2. For obstacle i with a user-specified boundary-uncertainty scale \sigma_i, and signed distance d_i(x) from its nominal boundary, the risk is r_i(x) = \exp(-d_i(x)^2/2\sigma_i^2). Treating each obstacle as an independent failure mode, the per-obstacle scores are fused into a single risk field, or RiskMap,
which is bounded in [0, 1], monotone in each r_i, and saturates as risk accumulates across nearby obstacles. This field
